questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [mid] database-backed feature flags and staged rollout (organized-study-cal-com, cal.diy/fabledocs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/06-architecture-critique.md). Scenario: a scheduling SaaS runs 30 app instances and takes about 5,000 bookings a minute at peak; customers are 18,000 teams grouped under 2,500 organizations, and some teams have sub-teams; about 20 flags are live at once, from week-long release toggles to permanent kill switches; next quarter you must roll out the team-permission fix behind a flag, first to your own team, then to a slice of organizations, then to everyone, and on-call must be able to switch a misbehaving feature off everywhere within a minute. Write your design before you look: where flag state lives and at which scopes, what 'no setting' means at each scope and which scope wins, how a check on the booking hot path avoids a database round trip, how a change reaches 30 instances, how the rollout stages are expressed, what an evaluation does when the flag store is down, how both sides of a flag get tested, and how a finished flag is retired. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Keep flag state in the database at three scopes: a global Feature row per slug (enabled, type, stale, last used, updated by), plus TeamFeatures and UserFeatures rows keyed by (team or user, feature) that record who assigned them. A flag then flips at runtime with no deploy, can target one team or one person, and leaves a trail of who changed it.

[w3] Make 'no setting' explicit with three states per scope: a row with enabled true is on, a row with enabled false is off, and no row means inherit from the scope above; setting a scope back to inherit deletes its row rather than storing false.

[w3] Write the precedence down and encode it in one place: for a user, an explicit user row decides; otherwise the user has the feature if a team they belong to has it enabled. Organizations are teams, so one org row covers its members without a row per person.

[w3] Keep the hot path off the database with a shared cache that the write path invalidates: the cached repository memoizes global lookups in Redis under per-slug and all-flags keys, and its update deletes exactly those keys, so a toggle made through it is visible to every instance on the next read instead of after an expiry.

[w2] Express rollout stages as targeting: rows for your own team first, then rows on chosen organizations (inherited down the hierarchy), then the global row. The schema has no percentage bucketing, so a 'slice of organizations' stage needs a deterministic hash of org id and flag slug, which keeps an org in its bucket on every request and every instance.

[w2] Decide what an evaluation does when the store fails: every check here reports the error to Sentry and rethrows, so a flag-store outage fails the requests that ask. A kill switch or a permission flag should instead fall to a declared safe value, so a store outage degrades the feature rather than the whole request.

[w2] Test both sides through the repository seam: consumers depend on an interface, so tests can swap the implementation. The shipped mock answers on only for the literal slug 'mock-feature' and always reports global flags on, so it cannot drive a real flag's on branch; a configurable fake that takes the answer per test can.

[w1] Retire flags deliberately: every slug is a key of one typed flag map, so deleting it from the type turns each remaining check into a compile error; remove the code paths first, then the rows. The stale marker and last-used time on the Feature row give flag debt a query instead of a guess.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — two months later: the bot-check flag is evaluated on every team booking at 5,000 bookings a minute; during a vendor outage on-call turns the bot-check flag's global row off, yet bookings for several teams keep going through the bot check; an organization enabled the permission fix org-wide, but members of one sub-team that had explicitly switched it off get the new behavior anyway; a flag deleted from the Feature table is still checked in code; and the flag integration suite has become flaky. What breaks, how would you notice, and what is the repair?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The booking route builds a fresh deprecated repository per request and the bot check asks it whether the team has the flag (checkIfTeamHasFeature) on every team booking; on that class the check has no cache, so each booking pays a unique-key lookup and, when the team has no row of its own, a recursive query up the team tree. Notice it in per-route query counts; repair by sending the check through a cached repository or evaluating once per team per minute.

[w3] The global row is not a kill switch here: the team check returns a team's own row if present and otherwise climbs the parent chain, and never reads the global Feature row, so switching it off changes nothing for teams with an enabled row. Repair: evaluate global-off as overriding every scope, or kill at the scope where it was enabled.

[w2] An explicit 'off' on a sub-team does not stop an org-level 'on' for its members: the user check's recursive query marks a team only for an enabled row and keeps climbing past a team whose row is disabled, so the org's enabled row wins. Asking about the team itself does honor its own disabled row, so the same setting means two things depending on the question. Pick one rule (does a disabled row block inheritance?) and test the three-level case.

[w2] A killed feature can stay alive per instance: the deprecated repository keeps every global flag in a static in-process copy for 5 minutes, and nothing clears it on update (its clear method is private and nothing calls it on update), so each of 30 instances flips on its own schedule within that window. Log the evaluated value with the flag so a lagging instance is visible; route all global reads through the invalidated shared cache.

[w2] A slug with no row is never cached: the memoize wrapper stores a result only when it is not null or undefined, so every check of a deleted flag (and every lookup that finds no row) goes to the database on every call. Removing data before code turns a cached check into a per-request query; remove the code first.

[w1] The flaky suite comes from process-wide cache state: the integration tests share the repository's static cache and reach into its private clear method between steps, so a test that reads flags before creating its own row sees a stale list. Inject the cache (or the clock) into the repository so each test starts clean.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your flag design against the alternatives: environment-variable switches versus database rows; a per-process memory cache versus a shared Redis cache; expiry-only caching versus invalidating on write; inherited org, team and user scopes versus flat per-team flags; shipping the flag map to the browser versus evaluating only on the server; and keeping the old code path alive behind a flag during a migration versus deleting it. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Environment variables cost no lookup and cannot fail at runtime, and the booking path gates whole-instance behavior on them, but changing one means a redeploy and it is all-or-nothing for the instance. Database rows change at runtime and target teams or users, at the price of a lookup that must be cached.

[w3] A per-process cache is the fastest read and survives a Redis outage, but each instance goes stale on its own and the write path cannot reach it; a shared Redis cache gives every instance one view at the cost of a network hop per check, and the memoize wrapper treats a failed Redis read or write as a miss and goes to the database, so the cache can slow a check but not break it.

[w2] Invalidating on write makes a change visible at once, but the delete runs after the write and a failed delete is only logged, so the expiry stays as the backstop that bounds staleness; expiry-only caching is simpler and is wrong for a kill switch, which must not wait out a TTL.

[w2] Inheritance lets one org row roll a feature out to hundreds of teams in a single write, at the cost of a recursive query per check and harder invalidation: a parent's change alters every descendant's answer, while the cached team repository keys and clears only a team's own rows, so it leaves the inherited check uncached. Flat per-team flags cache trivially but turn an org rollout into thousands of writes.

[w2] Shipping the flag map to the browser lets the UI hide unfinished screens, and its all-false fallback while loading keeps the old UI as the default; but the browser can be edited, so a client flag is a display switch only and the server must enforce anything that matters.

[w2] Keeping the old path behind a flag makes rollback a flip instead of a revert and deploy, at the price of two code paths that both need tests until the old one is deleted; the migration is not done until the flag and the old path are gone.
keyPoints.quote: keep old post-commit path behind flag

keyPoints.text: [w1] Choose each flag's default so that a missing row or a failed lookup lands on the safe side; a security fix should be phrased so that its safe behavior does not depend on a lookup succeeding.
keyPoints.quote: roll out behind a flag defaulting to deny
